summary:
Wisconsin is a state within the United States and stands under the country's national framework, which is carried by the national record. What follows is the Wisconsin-specific layer only.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Wisconsin in its low-risk group alongside Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Arizona and the District of Columbia, describing jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them. Wisconsin sits in that middle position: no state restriction on transgender people's use of facilities, no state ban on gender-affirming care, and no statewide nondiscrimination protection on gender identity.

As of May 2025 Wisconsin had no law barring transgender people from government-building bathrooms or facilities consistent with their gender identity, no law defining sex to exclude transgender people, and no restriction on drag performance. The Equality Map, which tracks state-level facility bans, records no such ban in Wisconsin.

Gender-affirming care for minors is not banned in Wisconsin. Governor Tony Evers vetoed Assembly Bill 465 on 6 December 2023 and, later the same month, a second legislature-passed bill barring such care for under-18s; a 2021 bill barring insurers from covering the procedures failed in committee. Wisconsin also did not enact a trans-athlete ban: Evers vetoed the bill on 2 April 2024, having promised the veto since its introduction, and the bill's sponsor called the decision disgusting.

Care access nonetheless narrowed under federal funding pressure. On 13 January 2026 UW Health and Children's Wisconsin each announced a pause on gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18 after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said it would deny Medicaid and Medicare payments to hospitals providing such care to minors. Mental and behavioural health services continued. Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul joined a coalition of states seeking to block the HHS declaration. The pause flows from federal pressure rather than any state ban, and Wisconsin has no shield law.

Wisconsin has no statewide nondiscrimination law covering gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. As of May 2025, 21% of the population was covered by full local ordinances in 10 cities and 12% by partial ordinances, so in most of the state a refusal of service or accommodation on grounds of gender identity has no state or local statutory remedy. The state hate-crime law covers sexual orientation but not gender identity, though prosecutors have used perceived sexual orientation as the medium to charge crimes motivated by a victim's gender identity.

State employment is covered. Executive Order #1, issued 7 January 2019, prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression in state employment, state contracting and the provision of state services, and directs state agencies to adopt and enforce nondiscrimination policies carrying those protections.

Since September 2023 the Milwaukee Police Department has stopped publishing the gender of crime victims, a change made to avoid misgendering transgender individuals in future reporting.
tangentialFactors:
The low-risk classification reflects the absence of targeting rather than active protection. Wisconsin's record is one of vetoes against a Republican-controlled legislature that repeatedly passed restriction bills: a trans-athlete bill passed the Assembly on party lines in 2021 and was never voted in the Senate, was reintroduced in 2023, and passed both houses in 2024 before veto; Democrats did not have the votes to stop passage in the legislature. A change of governor would remove that barrier, and the sources do not state the current legislative arithmetic.

October 2023 public hearings on bills to ban gender-affirming care for transgender youth, including the Help Not Harm Act built on model legislation, and to restrict transgender sports participation were marked by misinformation, with lawmaker questions indicating gaps in basic knowledge of the subject matter. The WIAA and NCAA retained their own policies addressing transgender athletes in the absence of a state rule.

Introductions of the athlete and medical-care bills drew sustained opposition from Fair Wisconsin, GSAFE and the ACLU of Wisconsin. In October 2023 Governor Evers, addressing "LGBTQ folks — especially our trans kids," said he would "veto any bill that makes Wisconsin a less welcoming, less inclusive, and less safe place for you to be who you are." A 2017 PRRI poll found 73% support for an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity against 20% opposed.

Wisconsin's position contrasts with the 27 states that ban gender-affirming care for children and the 9 states and 1 territory with school or government-building bathroom bans, while also falling short of the states that have enacted statewide gender-identity protections.
localsOnly:
Wisconsin has no statewide law covering gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations. Local ordinances fill part of the gap: Dane and Milwaukee counties and the cities of Appleton, Cudahy, De Pere, Janesville, Madison, Milwaukee and Racine ban gender-identity discrimination, while Oshkosh and Stevens Point ban discrimination against transgender city employees only. As of May 2025 these full and partial ordinances covered 21% and 12% of the population respectively.

Amending a Wisconsin birth certificate requires documentation of sex reassignment surgery and a name change; neither the birth certificate nor the driver's licence offers an X gender-neutral option, licence marker change is limited, and the name-change process is restrictive. People on Wisconsin's sex offender registry are barred from changing their names with no exception where the person is transgender.

Medicaid coverage of sex reassignment surgery had to be explicitly included for government employees from January 2019 and was ordered extended to non-government employees in May 2019 under the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment. A June 2023 budget bill passed by both houses that would have banned Medicaid coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming healthcare regardless of age was vetoed under line-item veto power. As of May 2025 private insurance and Medicaid were barred from excluding transgender-specific care.

People in Wisconsin prisons are entitled to hormone therapy. The 2005 Inmate Sex Change Prevention Act, which denied hormone therapy to prisoners undergoing sex reassignment, was ruled unanimously unconstitutional by the Seventh Circuit in Fields v. Smith on 5 August 2011, and the Supreme Court denied the state's appeal on 26 March 2012.

Conversion therapy on minors is banned in 14 communities, among them Milwaukee in March 2018, Madison in July 2018, Eau Claire in October 2018, West Allis in September 2020 and Kenosha in October 2020, where penalties reach a $1,000 fine plus costs, 90 days in Kenosha County Jail and suspension of driving privileges for up to five years. A June 2021 executive order barred state taxpayer dollars from funding conversion therapy on LGBT minors; statewide bans were blocked in June 2020 and January 2023, and in July 2025 the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled 4-3 that such bans can be enacted by regulation and executive order.

From 1 July 2021 Wisconsin birth certificates offer gender-neutral spouse and spouse or parent 1 and parent 2 options for children of same-sex couples. The Chapter 770 domestic partnership registry, established 2009, ended 1 April 2018.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the January 2026 pause on gender-affirming pharmacologic care at UW Health and Children's Wisconsin has since been lifted, narrowed or extended to other Wisconsin providers is not sourced and remains unresolved.

No source documents how Wisconsin agencies, police or courts have handled a gender-identity complaint under a local ordinance, so enforcement of the 10 full and 12 partial local ordinances is unverified. The coverage percentages date to May 2025 and may have shifted.

The July 2026 low-risk grouping is an external assessment rather than a legal guarantee, and no source records how a Wisconsin court would treat a gender-identity-based refusal of service in a locality without an ordinance.

Whether a future legislature could pass a care or sports restriction that survives veto is not addressed by the sources; they establish only that the governor in office between 2023 and 2024 blocked each measure presented.

Federal travel-document rules, entry screening, custody conditions and immigration-detention practice are carried by the national record and are not repeated here.
